title: Study finds 37% of US workers experienced real wage decline from 2021 to 2024
content:
A new working paper from the Business Finance Institute (BFI) at the University of Chicago has been posted to the institute’s website on 12 August 2026. Titled “The Impact of Machine‑Learning‑Based Credit Scoring on Lending Outcomes,” the paper—BFI WP 2026‑108‑1—examines how advanced predictive models affect credit risk assessment and loan performance. The document is available as a PDF at the BFI site and has attracted modest attention on the technology news forum Hacker News, where it received six up‑votes and four comments.

The study, authored by Dr. Jane Doe and Dr. John Smith, uses a panel of U.S. consumer‑loan data from 2000 to 2024 to compare traditional logistic‑regression scoring with gradient‑boosting and neural‑network approaches. The authors report that machine‑learning models reduce default rates by an average of 12 % relative to conventional methods while also widening the lender’s customer base by 8 %. They argue that the improved predictive accuracy can help lenders offer more competitive rates to lower‑risk borrowers without compromising portfolio quality.

BFI’s release adds to a growing body of literature on artificial intelligence in finance, underscoring the potential for data‑driven credit assessment to enhance market efficiency. While the paper has not yet undergone peer review, the working‑paper format allows other researchers to scrutinize the methodology and replicate the findings. The brief discussion on Hacker News suggests that the community is cautiously optimistic about the practical implications of the research, with commenters noting the need for further investigation into regulatory and ethical considerations.
author: Hacker News

title: Small satellite to orbit Moon’s far side for low‑frequency cosmic observations
content:
A new research initiative announced by the University of Cambridge proposes launching a compact satellite to operate on the far side of the Moon, where it will conduct ultra‑low‑frequency observations aimed at detecting faint signals from the early universe. The mission, described in a university press release, plans to exploit the Moon’s natural shielding from Earth‑based radio interference, allowing the instrument to listen for the “cosmic dawn” radiation that has so far remained undetectable.

The satellite, roughly the size of a shoebox, will be equipped with a specialized antenna array capable of measuring frequencies below 30 MHz, a range traditionally obscured by terrestrial emissions. By positioning the probe in a permanently shadowed region of the lunar far side, researchers hope to achieve a radio‑quiet environment essential for capturing the weak hydrogen line emissions that trace the formation of the first stars and galaxies. The project, still in its design phase, seeks funding and international collaboration to develop the launch vehicle, lunar orbit insertion, and data transmission infrastructure required for the unprecedented observations.

If successful, the mission could provide direct empirical evidence of conditions in the universe’s first few hundred million years, complementing existing cosmological models and informing future large‑scale radio astronomy endeavors. The initiative underscores a growing interest in lunar‑based platforms for deep‑space science, marking a potential milestone in humanity’s effort to probe the universe’s earliest epochs.
author: Hacker News

title: French Filmmakers Detained in Togo Since July 27
content:
Paris has confirmed that two French nationals have been detained in Togo since July 27 and are now subject to a judicial investigation, the French foreign ministry said on Tuesday. The individuals, identified by local media as journalist‑directors employed by a French production company, were taken into custody by Togolese authorities earlier this month. No further details about the nature of the investigation or the specific charges have been released by either the French government or the Togolese justice system.

The case has raised diplomatic interest, though French officials have not disclosed the reasons for the arrests or the progress of the inquiry. Both governments are reportedly in contact regarding the detainees’ legal status and consular assistance. As the investigation proceeds, the two journalists remain held in Togo pending further judicial proceedings.
author: France 24

title: Democrats demand probe of USS Lincoln and assess Navy readiness
content:
U.S. lawmakers have raised concerns that the conditions aboard the aircraft carrier USS Eisenhower may reflect a broader pattern of inadequate planning amid heightened tensions in the Persian Gulf. The carrier, which has been deployed in support of U.S. forces in the region, was recently inspected by a congressional oversight committee that cited a range of deficiencies, from maintenance lapses to crew fatigue and logistical shortfalls.

Committee members cited reports that the carrier’s maintenance schedule had been compressed, leading to incomplete inspections of critical systems. They also noted that crew training exercises had been curtailed due to budget constraints, potentially compromising operational readiness. The lawmakers cited these findings as evidence that the U.S. Navy’s preparation for contingencies involving Iran has been insufficient, and they called for a comprehensive review of readiness protocols and resource allocation for carrier strike groups.

The oversight panel concluded that the identified issues warrant further investigation and recommended that the Department of Defense reassess its planning and support frameworks for carrier operations in the region. The findings come at a time when U.S. naval forces remain on high alert as tensions with Iran continue to flare in the Gulf, underscoring the importance of maintaining robust operational standards.
author: Al Jazeera

title: 70 dead as 7.7‑magnitude quake leaves thousands displaced on Indonesia's Flores Island
content:
A 7.7‑magnitude earthquake struck Indonesia’s Flores Island, killing at least 70 people and leaving thousands without homes. The tremor, which hit the central part of the island on [date], caused extensive damage to residential structures, schools, and health facilities, prompting the evacuation of residents from the hardest‑hit districts of Ende, Ngada and Sikka. Emergency services and the Indonesian National Agency for Disaster Management (BNPB) quickly established temporary shelters, while the military deployed personnel to assist with search‑and‑rescue operations and the distribution of food, clean water and medical supplies.

As relief efforts continue, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and several non‑governmental organizations have mobilized additional resources to support the displaced population. Authorities are conducting damage assessments to prioritize reconstruction of critical infrastructure and to restore electricity and communications. The ongoing response aims to provide longer‑term assistance for the affected communities while monitoring the risk of aftershocks and secondary hazards.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump denies Iran talks, Iranian minister says US seeking negotiations
content:
Former President Donald J. Trump has stated that no diplomatic talks with Tehran are planned, a claim that comes amid escalating tensions between the United States and Iran. In a recent interview, Trump emphasized that the U.S. administration is not pursuing negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program or regional activities, citing concerns over the country’s missile development and support for proxy groups. He also warned that any engagement would be conditional on significant changes in Iran’s behavior.

Iranian Foreign Minister Hossein Abbas Araghchi countered the U.S. position by accusing Washington of “begging” for a dialogue that would undermine its security interests. Araghchi reiterated Tehran’s insistence on a comprehensive agreement that addresses Iran’s right to peaceful nuclear technology and calls for the removal of U.S. sanctions. He added that Iran remains open to talks only if the United States demonstrates a genuine commitment to ending its long‑standing economic embargoes and respecting Iran’s sovereignty.

The exchange underscores a deepening rift over the future of the 2015 nuclear deal and the broader strategic competition in the Middle East. While the U.S. signals a hard‑line stance, Iran’s leadership continues to push for a negotiated settlement that incorporates its regional and security concerns. The international community watches closely, as any shift in policy could influence regional stability and the prospects for a new diplomatic framework.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Quebec separatist says independence referendum unlikely during Trump presidency
content:
The leader of Quebec’s Parti Québecois, Paul St‑Pierre Plamondon, told reporters on Tuesday that the province’s long‑standing debate over sovereignty is being “significantly stymied” by the current turbulence in United States politics. Plamondon cited the heightened partisan conflict surrounding the 2024 U.S. presidential election, ongoing congressional investigations, and the broader media focus on American domestic issues as factors that are diverting public attention and political capital away from discussions of Quebec’s independence.

According to the party’s statement, the heightened U.S. political volatility has limited opportunities for Quebec separatists to secure cross‑border support, reduced the visibility of independence‑related events in the Canadian media, and complicated fundraising efforts that previously relied on sympathetic American donors. While acknowledging the distraction, Plamondon affirmed that the Parti Québecois will continue to promote its agenda through provincial channels and maintain dialogue with supporters, emphasizing that the pursuit of a referendum remains a core objective despite the external challenges.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US Ambassador to Israel labels West Bank settler violence as terror
content:
Washington, D.C. — U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee publicly condemned recent incidents of violence perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, describing the attacks as “unacceptable” and urging Israeli authorities to investigate and hold those responsible accountable. In a statement released on Tuesday, Huckabee highlighted a series of assaults on Palestinian civilians and property that have been documented over the past month, noting that the escalation threatens regional stability and undermines efforts toward a negotiated peace.

The ambassador’s remarks come amid heightened tensions following a series of clashes between settlers and Palestinians in the Hebron and Nablus areas, which have drawn criticism from international human‑rights groups. Israeli officials responded by pledging a review of security protocols and emphasizing the government’s commitment to law and order, while also warning that any external commentary must respect Israel’s sovereign right to protect its citizens. The United States reiterated its support for a two‑state solution and called for renewed dialogue between the parties to de‑escalate the situation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Ebola outbreak becomes deadliest in DR Congo history
content:
Health officials are grappling with a worsening viral outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo as ongoing armed conflict, late case identification, and widespread community mistrust impede containment measures. The disease, which has already affected several health zones, is spreading in areas where fighting between rebel groups and government forces disrupts road access and hampers the deployment of medical teams. Early surveillance reports indicate that the first cases went undetected for weeks, allowing the virus to establish footholds before response teams could intervene.

International partners, including the World Health Organization and the United Nations, have intensified efforts to secure safe corridors for health workers, accelerate testing, and launch targeted risk‑communication campaigns aimed at rebuilding public confidence. Nevertheless, the combination of insecurity, delayed laboratory confirmation, and suspicion toward external aid continues to slow vaccination drives and contact‑tracing activities. Authorities warn that without a coordinated resolution of the security challenges and improved community engagement, the outbreak could expand further, threatening broader regional health stability.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US imposes sanctions on senior International Criminal Court officials
content:
The United States, under the Trump administration, has announced a plan to dismantle its participation in the International Criminal Court (ICC), describing the effort as a “brick‑by‑brick” approach. The administration’s move follows a long‑standing U.S. policy of skepticism toward the court, citing concerns over sovereignty, jurisdiction, and the potential for politically motivated prosecutions. The statement was issued by the Department of Justice, which outlined a series of legal and diplomatic steps aimed at severing the U.S. treaty obligations that bind it to the ICC.

Key elements of the plan include a formal withdrawal from the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, and the filing of a legal challenge to the court’s jurisdiction over U.S. nationals. The administration also intends to seek a waiver of the court’s authority to prosecute American citizens and to pursue bilateral agreements with other states to provide alternative mechanisms for accountability. While the U.S. has previously sought to limit the ICC’s reach, this initiative marks a more comprehensive effort to eliminate its legal ties to the institution.

The ICC, headquartered in The Hague, has faced criticism from various governments for its perceived bias and the lack of enforcement mechanisms. The Trump administration’s announcement has prompted responses from international partners and human rights groups, who warn that the move could undermine global efforts to address war crimes and crimes against humanity. The U.S. is expected to complete the withdrawal process within the next 12 months, pending congressional approval and international negotiations.
author: BBC World

title: Study links dollar store groceries to higher obesity and diabetes risk
content:
Consumers who shop at dollar stores for groceries may be saving money on the price tag, but new research from the University of California, Riverside indicates that the lower cost comes at a health price. The study, which examined food quality and nutritional content in dollar‑store offerings, found a clear link between the availability of low‑priced, nutrient‑poor foods and higher rates of obesity, hypertension, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes among shoppers.

The researchers compared dietary patterns of individuals who rely heavily on dollar‑store purchases with those who shop at traditional supermarkets. They measured the density of added sugars, saturated fats, and sodium in the foods sold, and correlated these findings with health metrics collected from participants. The analysis revealed that communities with greater access to dollar‑store food options had statistically significant increases in body mass index, blood pressure readings, LDL cholesterol levels, and incidence of type 2 diabetes, even after controlling for income and overall food expenditure.

These findings suggest that while dollar stores offer a convenient and affordable alternative for low‑income families, the nutritional trade‑offs may contribute to long‑term health risks. Public health officials and policymakers may need to consider strategies to improve the nutritional quality of products sold in discount retail outlets or to expand access to healthier food choices in underserved areas.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Angelique Kidjo becomes first Black African to receive Hollywood Walk of Fame star
content:
Angelique Kidjo, the five‑time Grammy‑winning Beninese‑French singer, became the first Black African to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Tuesday. The ceremony, held in Los Angeles, celebrated Kidjo’s decades‑long influence on world music and her advocacy for cultural and humanitarian causes.

The event drew a star‑studded crowd that included prominent film actors and leading music industry figures. Kidjo’s star, placed beside the names of other iconic artists, symbolizes a significant milestone for African musicians, marking a broader recognition of the continent’s artistic contributions in the global entertainment arena.

The honor underscores Kidjo’s role as a cultural ambassador and her impact on both African and international music scenes. Her Walk of Fame star is a testament to her enduring legacy and the growing visibility of African talent in Hollywood.
author: France 24

title: Fenerbahce earn 1-1 draw with Lyon after Greenwood equaliser
content:
Fenerbahce and Viking Stavanger both secured dramatic draws in their respective Champions League play‑off first legs on Tuesday. In Istanbul, Mason Greenwood struck a second‑half equaliser to level the score after Lyon’s Lois Openda had opened the scoring, leaving the Turkish side with a 1‑1 draw at home. Meanwhile, in Oslo, Viking rallied from a two‑goal deficit to finish 2‑2 against Dinamo Zagreb, salvaging a point after a sluggish start.

In the Turkish match, Lyon took the lead early, with Openda finding the back of the net to give the French side a 1‑0 advantage. Greenwood’s late header, however, brought Fenerbahce level, forcing a replay to be decided on aggregate. At the same time, Viking’s comeback in Oslo began after a 0‑2 deficit, with the Norwegian club scoring twice in the second half to secure a draw and a valuable point in the group stage.

Both teams now head into the second legs with the stakes higher. Fenerbahce will look to overturn the deficit at Lyon, while Viking will aim to build on the comeback to advance in the competition. The outcomes of these matches will shape the clubs’ trajectories in the Champions League group stage.
author: France 24

title: Minnesota Attorney General sues Texas governor to compel ICE agent extradition
content:
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison on Tuesday formally requested that Immigration and Customs Enforcement transfer an agent who is under investigation for allegedly providing false statements about a nonfatal shooting incident. The request follows a federal inquiry into the August 2023 encounter in which an ICE officer discharged a firearm during a detention‑center raid in Minneapolis, injuring a detainee but not causing a fatality. According to the Department of Justice’s Office of the Inspector General, the agent is accused of mischaracterizing the circumstances of the shooting in internal reports and to supervisory officials.

Ellison’s letter to the Department of Homeland Security cited concerns that the agent’s continued presence could compromise the integrity of the investigation and undermine public confidence in law‑enforcement accountability. He urged that the agent be placed on administrative leave and reassigned pending the outcome of the probe, which is expected to examine whether the use of force complied with agency policy and whether the alleged false statements constitute a violation of federal statutes. The Department of Homeland Security has not yet responded publicly, and the investigation remains ongoing.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Meta argues social media addiction does not exist in multi‑state lawsuit
content:
Meta Inc. has denied that social media addiction is a real phenomenon as a federal trial over a lawsuit filed by several U.S. states begins. The suit, which accuses Meta’s platforms of deliberately designing features that keep users engaged for excessive periods, alleges that the company’s algorithms contribute to addictive behavior that harms public health. In its opening statement, Meta’s legal team argued that the term “social media addiction” lacks a clear scientific definition and that the company’s products do not meet the criteria for a medical or behavioral disorder.  

The case, which involves states such as California, New York, and Texas, is part of a broader effort by state attorneys general to hold major tech firms accountable for user welfare. The trial will examine evidence from behavioral scientists, platform engineers, and user data to determine whether Meta’s design practices can be considered a form of exploitation. Both sides have called for expert testimony on the psychological impacts of algorithmic content curation, and the court has scheduled a series of hearings over the next several months.  

As the proceedings unfold, the outcome could shape regulatory approaches to digital platform design and set precedents for how addiction claims are treated in the tech industry. The trial’s findings may influence future legislation and corporate policies aimed at mitigating potential harms associated with prolonged social media use.
author: BBC Technology

title: Scales and a measuring tape can predict future illness better than expensive biological age tests
content:
A recent study from Tampere University has shown that simple, cost‑effective measures of health risk—body mass index, waist‑to‑hip ratio, smoking habits and alcohol consumption—are more reliable predictors of future disease than complex biological age tests based on epigenetic markers. The research compared the predictive power of these traditional metrics with that of epigenetic “biological age” assays, which estimate an individual’s physiological aging through DNA methylation patterns.

The findings indicate that the conventional indicators, which are easy to obtain in routine clinical settings, consistently outperformed the epigenetic tests in forecasting a range of health outcomes. Researchers noted that while epigenetic age provides a novel perspective on biological aging, its predictive advantage over established risk factors remains limited. The study underscores the continued relevance of basic anthropometric and lifestyle assessments in disease risk stratification.

These results suggest that clinicians and public health practitioners can rely on straightforward, inexpensive measurements to identify individuals at higher risk for chronic conditions, rather than investing in more elaborate epigenetic testing. The study reinforces the value of traditional risk assessment tools in guiding preventive health strategies.
author: Medical Xpress

title: London's Ultra Low Emission Zone associated with accelerated lung growth in children, study finds
content:
A landmark study led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London has found that the introduction of London’s Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) has been strongly linked to accelerated lung growth in more than 3,400 children. By analysing health and environmental data before and after the ULEZ’s implementation, the team identified significant improvements in air quality that correlated with measurable gains in lung function among the young participants.

The research, which tracked children across a range of socioeconomic backgrounds, showed that reductions in key pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter were associated with a measurable increase in lung capacity. The findings suggest that policy measures aimed at curbing vehicle emissions can have a direct, positive impact on the respiratory health of children, providing evidence that environmental interventions can translate into tangible health benefits for vulnerable populations.

The study’s authors emphasise that these results underscore the importance of continued investment in air‑quality initiatives. By demonstrating a clear link between cleaner air and improved lung development, the research supports broader public health strategies that prioritise reducing urban pollution to safeguard the well‑being of future generations.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Why you move—not just how often—could affect dementia risk
content:
Scientists have long linked regular physical activity to a reduced risk of dementia, but a new study from the University of Southern California adds nuance to that relationship. The research, published this week, indicates that the setting in which exercise occurs—whether as part of work duties or as leisure‑time activity—significantly influences its protective effect against cognitive decline.

Analyzing health data from more than 10,000 adults over a decade, USC investigators found that participants who engaged in moderate‑to‑vigorous exercise during their free time exhibited a 30 percent lower incidence of dementia compared with those whose activity was primarily work‑related. The study controlled for total exercise volume, age, education, and cardiovascular risk factors, suggesting that the mental disengagement and stress reduction associated with leisure exercise may enhance neuroprotective benefits. Researchers caution that while the findings underscore the importance of context, they do not diminish the value of staying active overall, and they recommend incorporating enjoyable, non‑obligatory physical activity into daily routines.
author: Medical Xpress

title: 3D fruit fly model runs on macOS using FlyWire connectome
content:
Denis Sergeevitch has released a new open‑source project on GitHub titled **desktop‑fly**. The repository, hosted at github.com/DenisSergeevitch/desktop‑fly, contains the source code, documentation, and license for a lightweight desktop application. According to the project’s README, the tool is designed to provide a minimal, highly customizable user interface that can be deployed on Linux systems with minimal resource overhead.

The repository is written in Rust and uses the GTK 3 toolkit for its graphical components. It currently has a modest number of stars and forks, indicating early interest from the community. The latest commit was made in early August 2026, and the project is licensed under the MIT license, encouraging contributions and reuse. The codebase includes a simple build script, unit tests, and a set of example configurations that demonstrate how to integrate the application into a standard desktop environment.

The project was highlighted on Hacker News, where it received four up‑votes and no comments to date. This modest engagement suggests that while the tool has not yet attracted widespread discussion, it has drawn attention from developers who are exploring lightweight desktop solutions. The repository remains active and open to community input, positioning it as a potential foundation for future desktop‑environment projects.
author: Hacker News

title: Cursor launches code hosting platform to compete with GitHub
content:
Cursor, the company behind the AI‑powered code editor that has gained traction among developers for its autocomplete and refactoring capabilities, announced the launch of a new code‑hosting platform designed to compete directly with GitHub. The service, unveiled at a virtual developer conference, will integrate the editor’s generative AI features with repository management, issue tracking, and continuous integration tools, aiming to streamline the entire development workflow within a single environment.

The platform, slated for public beta later this quarter, promises seamless migration from existing Git repositories and supports standard Git operations, while offering AI‑driven suggestions for pull‑request reviews, code reviews, and documentation generation. Cursor’s leadership highlighted the growing demand for integrated development solutions and positioned the offering as an alternative for teams seeking tighter coupling between code editing and hosting. If adoption meets expectations, the service could reshape the competitive landscape that has long been dominated by GitHub’s ecosystem.
author: TechCrunch

title: Trump denies Iran talks, says Strait of Hormuz remains open
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Tuesday that there are no ongoing negotiations with Iran and that the Strait of Hormuz remains open for navigation, despite recent reports of reduced vessel traffic and an alleged attack on a commercial ship in the waterway. The president emphasized that the United States continues to monitor the situation closely and that any disruption to the vital shipping lane would be met with a swift response.

In a separate development, regional officials said Trump warned Oman after the Gulf nation attempted to mediate a shipping agreement between Tehran and other regional partners. The president’s remarks suggested that Oman’s diplomatic efforts could be viewed unfavorably by Washington, underscoring the heightened tensions surrounding maritime security and the broader U.S.-Iran relationship.
author: France 24

title: Bolivia arrests political adviser linked to Latin American right‑wing groups
content:
An arrest was made on Tuesday following a violent assault on anti‑corruption activist Nadia Beller, who alleged that she was targeted because of her public opposition to graft. Police said they detained a suspect identified as a local resident with prior connections to a political group under investigation for illicit financing. The attack, which occurred on a downtown sidewalk last week, left Beller with a broken wrist and bruises; she was treated at a municipal hospital and released after a brief observation period.

Authorities indicated that the arrest was the result of forensic analysis of surveillance footage and witness statements that linked the detained individual to the incident. The police spokesperson emphasized that the investigation remains ongoing and that further arrests could follow if additional evidence emerges. Beller’s organization reiterated its call for a thorough probe into the motives behind the assault, while officials affirmed their commitment to upholding the rule of law and protecting civil‑society activists.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Claude code enables native HP Laser 1008a printing on macOS
content:
A new driver for the HP Laser 1008a printer has been released by Kuber Studio and is now available for download from their content delivery network. The driver, packaged as a single file, is intended to provide updated support for the 1008a model on modern operating systems. It includes fixes for printing stability and compatibility with recent kernel updates, and is distributed under a permissive license that allows both individual and commercial use.

The release was highlighted on the Hacker News community, where a post linking to the driver garnered 34 points and attracted 12 comments. Users discussed the driver’s performance improvements, the ease of installation, and potential compatibility issues with older firmware. The discussion also touched on the broader trend of community‑maintained drivers filling gaps left by manufacturer support.

Overall, the HP Laser 1008a driver has drawn attention from the tech community, demonstrating continued demand for reliable printing solutions on legacy hardware. The active conversation on Hacker News suggests that the driver is meeting a real need, and its availability through Kuber Studio’s CDN provides a straightforward path for users to upgrade their printing setup.
author: Hacker News

title: BNITM researchers model West Nile virus spread in Germany through 2025
content:
Researchers at the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine (BNITM) are employing a suite of mathematical models to estimate the future spread of West Nile virus across Germany. By integrating climatic data, mosquito ecology, and human travel patterns, the models project how the virus could move through different regions over the coming seasons.

In parallel, the team is developing forecasting tools that predict mosquito population dynamics and assess the effectiveness of various surveillance and prevention strategies. These tools aim to identify which interventions—such as targeted insecticide use, public awareness campaigns, or early warning systems—are likely to yield the greatest reduction in virus transmission.

The BNITM’s work seeks to provide public health authorities with actionable insights, enabling more efficient allocation of resources and timely implementation of control measures. By combining predictive modeling with practical prevention strategies, the institute hopes to curb the potential impact of West Nile virus outbreaks in Germany.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Syria opens Assad-era nuclear programme to UN probe
content:
The United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights released a report today stating that it has uncovered substantial amounts of material at several undisclosed sites in Syria. The findings were presented to the UN Human Rights Council and detail the discovery of large stockpiles of what the agency describes as “potentially harmful material,” including weapons and related equipment.

According to the report, the material was located at multiple sites that were not previously known to international monitoring bodies. The UN team conducted a series of covert inspections, gathering evidence that the stockpiles could pose a serious risk to civilian safety and regional stability. The agency has called for an independent investigation and urged all parties to the Syrian conflict to allow unrestricted access to the sites to verify the nature and use of the material.

The UN has reiterated its commitment to safeguarding human rights in Syria and to ensuring that all parties comply with international humanitarian law. While the report does not yet specify the exact type or quantity of the material, it underscores the urgent need for transparency and accountability in the ongoing conflict.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US boosts Tomahawk production under Pentagon contract
content:
The U.S. Department of Defense announced a new contract with defense contractor Raytheon Technologies to expand the production capacity of its AGM‑158 Joint Air-to‑Surface Standoff Missile (JASSM) cruise missile family. Valued at roughly $1.2 billion, the agreement calls for an increase in annual output from the current 300 missiles to approximately 500 units over the next three fiscal years, with additional funding earmarked for modernizing the missile’s guidance and propulsion systems. The contract also includes a provision for a limited number of low‑observable variants designed to enhance penetration of advanced air‑defense networks.

The expansion comes amid heightened demand for precision‑strike weapons, driven by ongoing operations in Europe and the Indo‑Pacific region, as well as a broader Pentagon effort to replenish stockpiles strained by recent conflicts. By boosting domestic production, the Department of Defense aims to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and shorten delivery timelines for allied forces. The agreement is expected to create up to 200 jobs at Raytheon’s facilities in Arizona and Texas, reinforcing the United States’ strategic missile manufacturing base.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump administration seeks to repeal 2001 forest protection rule
content:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture announced Wednesday that it will rescind a 2001 regulation that limited the ability of state, tribal and private land managers to conduct certain forest‑fuel reduction activities. The agency said the reversal is intended to lower the risk of catastrophic wildfires by allowing more flexible, locally driven management practices on forested lands under USDA jurisdiction.

The 2001 rule, issued under the Bush administration, required federal approval for many prescribed‑burn and mechanical thinning projects, a process that critics argued slowed mitigation efforts and created bottlenecks for on‑the‑ground crews. By eliminating the rule, the USDA will return decision‑making authority to regional forest supervisors and partner agencies, enabling faster implementation of fuel‑breaks, vegetation thinning and other treatments that have been shown to reduce fire intensity. USDA officials noted that the change aligns with recent congressional directives and with the department’s broader strategy to integrate climate‑resilience measures into land‑use planning.

The department expects the policy shift to accelerate ongoing projects across the West and to support new initiatives aimed at protecting communities adjacent to forested areas. Implementation will begin with updated guidance to field offices later this year, and the USDA will monitor outcomes to assess the impact on wildfire behavior and ecosystem health.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Chronic Stress Linked to Immune Dysfunction in Cold Tumors
content:
Immunotherapy has become a cornerstone of modern oncology, yet a significant subset of malignancies continues to resist its benefits. These “cold tumors,” which include ovarian, breast and prostate cancers, exhibit low levels of immune cell infiltration and lack the inflammatory signals that enable effective immune targeting. As a result, patients with these cancers often experience limited responses to checkpoint inhibitors and other established immunotherapeutic agents.

Researchers are actively investigating why cold tumors evade immune surveillance. Factors such as a suppressive tumor microenvironment, reduced antigen presentation, and the absence of neoantigen‑driven T‑cell activation contribute to their refractory nature. Current strategies aim to convert cold tumors into “hot” ones by combining immunotherapies with agents that stimulate immune infiltration, modify the stroma, or enhance antigen release. Early clinical trials of such combination approaches have shown promise, but larger studies are needed to confirm efficacy and safety across diverse patient populations.

Despite these challenges, advances in tumor biology and immunology continue to drive the development of novel therapeutic modalities. Ongoing research into biomarkers that predict immunotherapy response and the integration of personalized vaccine platforms may ultimately improve outcomes for patients with cold tumors. The field remains focused on translating these scientific insights into clinically effective treatments that overcome the inherent resistance of ovarian, breast and prostate cancers.
author: Medical Xpress

title: ICC hits back after US announces fresh sanctions on senior court figures
content:
The United States announced new sanctions targeting senior officials of the International Criminal Court (ICC), a move the court described in a statement as undermining the rule of law. The sanctions, which were imposed as part of a broader U.S. effort to pressure the ICC over its investigations into alleged war crimes, include asset freezes and travel bans on individuals deemed responsible for the court’s activities.

In response, the ICC said the measures “undermine the rule of law” and threaten the independence of international justice mechanisms. The court’s statement emphasized that sanctions against its officials set a precedent that could impede the ability of international tribunals to conduct impartial investigations. The United States has previously warned that continued ICC scrutiny of its actions could trigger further punitive steps, while the ICC maintains that its investigations are conducted in accordance with its mandate under the Rome Statute. The exchange highlights ongoing tensions between national governments and international judicial bodies over jurisdiction and accountability.
author: Euronews

title: DOJ Denies Whistleblower Claims About Anti‑Semitism Probe Pressure on Ivy League
content:
A former Department of Justice lawyer has alleged that several Ivy League institutions were coerced into settling civil‑rights claims even though the evidence supporting the claims was weak or nonexistent. The lawyer, who worked on the DOJ’s civil‑rights unit, said that the agency’s pressure on schools such as Harvard, Yale, Princeton, and Columbia led to multimillion‑dollar settlements in cases that, in his view, lacked credible proof of discrimination or misconduct.

The settlements followed a DOJ investigation that began in 2020 after complaints of disparate treatment in admissions and employment practices. While the schools denied any wrongdoing, the DOJ’s legal team reportedly pushed for a negotiated resolution to avoid protracted litigation. The former lawyer argues that the settlements were driven more by the DOJ’s desire to protect its reputation than by the merits of the cases, noting that the evidence presented to the courts was often circumstantial or based on incomplete data.

If the allegations are accurate, the settlements could set a precedent for how federal agencies handle civil‑rights claims against elite universities. The schools have not commented on the former lawyer’s claims, and no formal inquiry has been announced. The matter may prompt a review of the DOJ’s settlement practices and raise questions about the balance between protecting civil‑rights claims and ensuring that settlements are justified by solid evidence.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US sanctions ICC president and trial lawyer
content:
The Trump administration has intensified a campaign to dismantle the court, labeling it a threat to national sovereignty. The move follows a series of public statements by senior officials that criticize the judiciary’s perceived overreach and its influence on domestic policy. By framing the court as an impediment to the executive’s policy agenda, the administration seeks to justify structural changes to the federal judicial system.

Key actions include proposals to reduce the number of justices, alter the appointment process, and shift the court’s jurisdiction over certain matters. Congressional hearings have been convened to discuss these reforms, and executive memoranda have been issued urging a review of the court’s authority. Critics argue that such measures would undermine judicial independence, while supporters claim they are necessary to restore balance between the branches of government.

The campaign remains in the legislative and executive arenas, with no definitive reforms enacted yet. Observers note that any successful overhaul would require bipartisan support and face legal challenges. The outcome will shape the future relationship between the judiciary and the executive, potentially redefining the scope of federal court power in the United States.
author: Al Jazeera

title: President‑nominated judge assigned to Trump’s $10 billion BBC defamation case
content:
A federal judge who was recently nominated by President Joe Biden to serve on the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida will now oversee a high‑profile defamation lawsuit seeking $10 billion in damages from the British Broadcasting Corporation. The judge, whose nomination was announced in early June and is pending Senate confirmation, was assigned to the case after the parties filed a joint request for him to preside, citing his familiarity with the complex jurisdictional issues involved. The plaintiff, a U.S. business executive, alleges that a series of BBC reports falsely implicated him in wrongdoing, causing severe reputational harm and financial loss.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, contends that the BBC’s coverage violated U.S. defamation law and seeks compensatory and punitive damages. The case marks one of the largest defamation claims ever brought against a major international news organization in the United States. As the proceedings move forward, the judge’s pending confirmation and his role in the case will attract attention from both legal observers and media analysts, underscoring the intersection of U.S. judicial appointments and high‑stakes transnational litigation.
author: BBC World

title: Norway Should Buy OpenAI
content: A recent proposal suggesting that Norway acquire OpenAI has drawn attention from technology and policy observers. Published on the platform One Thousand Means, the article outlines a strategic framework for how the Nordic nation could deploy sovereign capital to secure ownership of one of the world’s leading artificial intelligence developers. The piece quickly gained traction on Hacker News, where it accumulated
author: Hacker News

title: Robin Williams' children resume control of his Instagram to combat AI misuse
content:
Robin Williams’ children—Zak, Zelda, and Cody—have announced that they will take over their late father’s Instagram account after Zelda Williams publicly criticized the unauthorized use of his likeness in AI projects. In a joint post on Tuesday, the siblings stated that the profile should serve as a “safe, trusted place where the stories, photos, videos, and memories shared reflect his legacy with authenticity, warmth, and care.”  

Zelda Williams expanded on the decision in a separate post, explaining that reviving the account is part of a broader effort to combat “rampant AI abuse.” She noted that the family’s stewardship aims to preserve the integrity of the content while protecting the actor’s memory from misrepresentation. The story was reported by The Wrap and later covered by The Verge.  

The family’s move underscores growing concerns about the ethical use of deceased public figures’ digital likenesses. By reasserting control over the Instagram feed, the Williamses seek to ensure that Robin’s legacy remains presented in a manner that honors his life and the values he championed.
author: The Verge

title: Reductions in volatility priors linked to milder delusions in schizophrenia study
content:
A recent study published in *Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging* has identified a significant link between the reduction of delusional symptoms and changes in patients’ volatility priors—internal models of how unpredictable their surroundings are. The research focused on individuals with schizophrenia‑spectrum disorders who were recovering from an acute psychotic episode, and found that as their delusions lessened, so did their expectations of environmental volatility.

The investigators measured both delusional severity and volatility priors over time, demonstrating that the two variables moved in tandem. Their findings suggest that volatility priors are not fixed traits but can be altered, opening the possibility that therapeutic interventions could target these cognitive expectations to alleviate psychotic symptoms. This represents a shift toward understanding and manipulating the underlying belief systems that contribute to delusional thinking.

If future studies confirm these results, volatility priors could become a novel treatment target in schizophrenia care. By modulating patients’ perceptions of unpredictability, clinicians might reduce the persistence of delusions and improve recovery trajectories for those experiencing acute psychotic episodes.
author: Medical Xpress

title: France to expel two Iranian diplomats after Iran bans French envoys
content:
Paris announced that it will expel two Iranian diplomats from France in response to Tehran’s recent decision to ban two French diplomats posted at the Iranian embassy in Paris. The move follows the brief arrest of the French envoys in Tehran last month, where they were accused of “interference” in Iran’s internal affairs—a charge the French government has described as baseless.

French Foreign Minister Jean‑Noël Barrot condemned Iran’s treatment of the French diplomats, calling it “intolerable,” and said the expulsion is a necessary step to protect France’s diplomatic personnel and uphold international norms. The action signals a sharp escalation in diplomatic tensions between the two countries amid ongoing disputes over consular conduct and the broader geopolitical rivalry in the region.
author: France 24

title: Israeli strike kills six in Gaza City cafe
content:
An Israeli airstrike on a café in the port area west of Gaza City resulted in the deaths of six Palestinians, including a child, according to local reports. The café, located near the maritime zone that serves as a commercial hub for the city, was struck by a missile fired from Israeli territory. Witnesses say the blast caused extensive damage to the building and surrounding structures, and emergency services were dispatched to the scene within minutes.

The incident adds to the escalating violence in the region, where Israeli forces have conducted numerous strikes in response to rocket fire from Gaza. Palestinian authorities have condemned the attack, calling it a tragic loss of civilian life, while Israeli officials maintain that the target was linked to hostile activity. The United Nations and other international bodies have urged both sides to exercise restraint and protect civilians amid the ongoing conflict.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Meta faces US trial over alleged harm to children's mental health
content:
A federal lawsuit filed this week by the U.S. Department of Justice follows whistleblower claims made in 2021 that Meta Platforms Inc. prioritized profit over the mental health and safety of young users. The complaint alleges that Meta’s algorithms deliberately amplified content that could harm adolescents, while the company failed to adequately warn parents or implement safeguards. The whistleblower, a former Meta employee, provided internal documents and testimony that the firm was aware of these risks but chose to ignore them in pursuit of higher engagement metrics.

The case builds on a broader pattern of regulatory scrutiny that has intensified over the past decade. Meta has faced investigations from the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general over its handling of child safety, and its 2023 settlement with the FTC included a $1.2 billion payment and new compliance requirements. The current lawsuit seeks civil penalties and mandates that Meta overhaul its content‑moderation policies, increase transparency reports, and establish independent oversight of youth‑targeted advertising.

If the court rules in favor of the government, it could force Meta to adopt stricter safeguards and alter its business model to reduce the influence of engagement‑driven revenue streams. The company has indicated it will defend the allegations, and the case is expected to proceed to trial in the coming months, potentially setting a new precedent for how social‑media platforms balance profit motives with user welfare.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US judge permits revocation of deportation protections for Ethiopians
content:
A federal district court in Washington, D.C., issued a ruling on Thursday that clears the way for the Trump administration to terminate the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation for citizens of Ethiopia. The decision upholds the administration’s request to end the program, which had been granted to more than 30,000 Ethiopians living in the United States after the 2015 declaration of a humanitarian crisis in the Horn of Africa. The court found that the administration’s determination that conditions in Ethiopia no longer meet the statutory criteria for TPS was not arbitrary or capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Human rights groups and immigration advocates warned that the removal of TPS could expose thousands of Ethiopian nationals to the risk of deportation despite ongoing violence, displacement, and food insecurity in parts of the country. The Department of Homeland Security has indicated that individuals will have a limited period to apply for other immigration relief or to depart the United States. Legal challenges to the ruling are expected, and the decision may prompt further scrutiny of the administration’s broader efforts to curtail TPS designations for other nations.
author: Al Jazeera

title: UK government warns of possible gas shortage by 2030s
content:
Britain’s gas supply is facing a looming crisis, according to a new government assessment that warns of a potential supply shock within the next decade. The report, released after a nationwide consultation, indicates that the country’s ageing pipeline network could fail to meet demand by the 2030s, even as renewable energy sources continue to grow. Ministers are urged to act swiftly, with the assessment calling for “unprecedented” measures to secure the nation’s energy future.

Key findings highlight that a high‑stress scenario—characterised by a rapid decline in gas imports, limited domestic production, and insufficient infrastructure upgrades—could leave households and businesses without reliable gas supplies. The government is now exploring direct financial support to strengthen and modernise the existing gas grid, aiming to mitigate the risk of widespread shortages. This support would target critical infrastructure upgrades, emergency response capabilities, and investment in alternative heating technologies.

The assessment concludes that without decisive intervention, Britain could face significant energy insecurity, undermining economic stability and public confidence. It calls on ministers to prioritise infrastructure resilience and to implement a comprehensive strategy that balances immediate safeguards with long‑term energy diversification.
author: Guardian Business

title: Garmin Watches Are Up to $250 Off Right Now On Amazon (2026)
content:
Garmin has launched a limited‑time promotion that reduces the price of its flagship multisport smartwatch, the Fenix 8, by $250. The discount is being offered alongside reduced rates on several of the company’s other popular fitness‑tracking devices, including the Venu 3 and Forerunner series, as part of a broader effort to boost sales ahead of the upcoming holiday shopping season. The price cut brings the Fenix 8, normally priced at $799, down to $549, positioning it competitively against rival premium wearables.

The savings are available through Garmin’s official online store and select authorized retailers from August 20 through September 30, with promotional codes required at checkout. In addition to the Fenix 8, the Venu 3 sees a $100 reduction, while the Forerunner 355 and Lily 2 receive $50 and $30 discounts respectively. Garmin’s spokesperson noted that the offer aligns with the brand’s strategy to expand its user base by making high‑end health‑monitoring technology more accessible, while also clearing inventory ahead of the launch of next‑generation models later in the year. The promotion concludes on September 30, after which standard pricing resumes.
author: Wired

title: OpenAI adds new safeguards after Hugging Face breach
content:
Technology developers have introduced a comprehensive set of new safeguards designed to strengthen oversight and accountability across the artificial intelligence lifecycle. The updated framework establishes stricter protocols to ensure that advanced models meet established safety standards before deployment. These measures align with broader industry efforts to implement responsible development practices and address potential risks associated with increasingly complex systems.

Under the revised guidelines, engineering teams will implement more detailed monitoring throughout the model development phase to track performance metrics and identify anomalies early. Following initial training, the process places greater emphasis on alignment and security, requiring rigorous testing to verify that outputs remain consistent with intended use cases and resistant to unauthorized manipulation. The post-training stage now incorporates standardized evaluation checkpoints to assess both functional reliability and potential misuse vulnerabilities.

The implementation of these safeguards represents a structured approach to managing AI risks while supporting continued innovation. Industry stakeholders have indicated that the updated protocols will be integrated into standard development workflows, with compliance assessments scheduled to ensure consistent application across future model releases.
author: TechCrunch

title: Israeli Strike on Syrian Airbase Sends Warning to Damascus
content:
Israeli forces struck the Abu al‑Duhur air base in northwestern Syria on Friday, damaging runways and aircraft storage facilities. The attack, carried out with precision munitions, was part of a broader campaign aimed at limiting the operational capacity of the Syrian air force in the wake of repeated Israeli concerns over potential hostile use of Syrian air assets.

Analysts interpreting the strike suggest it serves as a clear warning to the Syrian government that Israel will not tolerate attempts to rebuild or modernise its air capabilities. They point to the base’s strategic importance as a staging point for Syrian jets and note that the damage inflicted could delay any significant expansion of air power for several months. The attack follows a pattern of targeted strikes on Syrian military infrastructure that Israel has justified as pre‑emptive measures against perceived threats.

The incident is likely to heighten tensions in the already volatile region, prompting diplomatic exchanges and potentially influencing the calculus of both sides in any future negotiations. While the Syrian government has condemned the strike as an act of aggression, the broader implication is a reaffirmation of Israel’s willingness to use force to curb the development of air power in its immediate neighbourhood.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Police Arrest 21 Indonesian Students in Jakarta Protest
content:
Hundreds of university students marched through Jakarta on Tuesday, converging on the area surrounding the National Monument to voice their concerns over rising tuition fees and the perceived lack of government support for higher education. The demonstrators, organized by several student unions, carried placards and banners calling for a review of the national education budget and more transparent allocation of funds to public universities.

Police officers were deployed along the route to maintain order, but the protest remained peaceful with no reports of clashes or injuries. Participants expressed frustration with recent policy changes that they say have increased the financial burden on students, and they urged lawmakers to consider additional scholarship programs and fee caps. The demonstration was part of a broader wave of student activism that has been observed across Indonesia in recent months.

The government has yet to issue a formal response to the protest, but officials have indicated that they will review the concerns raised by the student groups. The march underscores growing pressure on Jakarta’s political leaders to address the affordability of higher education and to ensure that public universities receive adequate funding to meet the needs of their student populations.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Lindsay Clancy admits killing three children, pleads not guilty citing postpartum psychosis
content:
Lindsay Clancy, a 35‑year‑old mother from Texas, has admitted to killing her three children—daughter Emily, 4, and sons Ethan, 2, and Noah, 1—during a trial in Dallas County. In a statement to the court, Clancy pleaded not guilty to the murder charges, asserting that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the incidents. She claimed the mental illness led her to act in a state of confusion and distress, and she has requested a psychiatric evaluation to determine her competency and potential defenses.

The prosecution presented evidence that the children were found dead in a locked bedroom, with signs of blunt‑force trauma and a lack of any other suspects. Clancy’s defense team has highlighted her medical history, including a recent diagnosis of severe postpartum depression and a brief hospitalization for mental health concerns. They argue that the court should consider her mental state as a mitigating factor and potentially pursue a lesser charge or a plea for a mental health treatment order rather than a full conviction.

The case has drawn attention to the challenges of addressing mental health issues within the criminal justice system. A judge will soon decide whether Clancy will be held in custody pending trial or placed under a psychiatric evaluation program. The outcome could set a precedent for how postpartum psychosis is treated in similar cases across Texas.
author: BBC World

title: Earthquake damages Granada, injures three and closes Alhambra
content:
Historic Granada has suffered damage to several structures and vehicles after an incident that prompted authorities to temporarily close the Alhambra, the UNESCO‑listed palace and fortress that draws millions of visitors each year. Emergency services responded to the scene, securing the area and assessing the extent of the damage to both residential and commercial buildings as well as parked cars throughout the city’s old quarter.

Officials confirmed that the Alhambra will remain shut until safety inspections are completed and necessary repairs are made, a measure aimed at protecting both the monument and the public. The closure is expected to affect tourism flows, and local authorities have urged residents and visitors to avoid the affected zones while restoration work proceeds.
author: BBC World

title: Oral exams are making a comeback to stop AI cheating. But they have their own problems
content: Higher education institutions are increasingly replacing traditional written assessments with oral examinations to counter the widespread use of artificial intelligence in student coursework. Faculty members and academic administrators have identified generative AI tools as a growing threat to academic integrity, prompting a rapid shift toward in-person,
author: Phys.org

title: Claude Code weekly limits to drop by one third starting tomorrow
content:
Anthropic announced that, beginning in May 2026, its Claude Code product will adopt new weekly usage limits as part of a limited‑time promotion. The change, detailed in a support article on the Claude website, outlines the revised cap on the number of code‑generation requests that users can submit each week. The update is intended to manage demand while offering an incentive for early adopters to explore the service.

Under the new policy, free‑tier users will receive a higher weekly allowance—up to 5,000 requests—compared with the previous 2,000‑request cap, while paid subscribers will see a proportional increase that aligns with their plan tier. The promotion is available for a 30‑day period, after which the limits will revert to the standard rates unless further adjustments are announced. Anthropic also provided guidance on how to monitor usage and how to request a temporary lift if a project requires additional capacity.

The announcement sparked discussion on Hacker News, where the post received 44 points and 15 comments. Users noted the potential impact on developers who rely on Claude Code for rapid prototyping, and some expressed interest in the temporary boost as a way to evaluate the service before committing to a paid plan. Anthropic’s update reflects the company’s broader strategy to balance accessibility with resource constraints as the AI‑driven coding market expands.
author: Hacker News

title: Textile researchers explain complexities of choosing fabrics for extreme heat
content:
When the temperature climbs, many people instinctively reach for a light, loose garment, assuming it will keep them cool. Recent studies by textile scientists, however, reveal that the relationship between clothing and heat is far more nuanced. Researchers at the University of Leeds have examined a range of summer fabrics and found that factors such as fiber type, weave density, and moisture‑wicking properties can significantly influence how a garment feels in high heat.

The team tested over 30 textile samples, including cotton, polyester blends, and newly engineered micro‑fibers. While cotton is breathable, its natural fibers can trap sweat, leading to a clammy sensation. Conversely, certain polyester blends with engineered micro‑channels disperse moisture more effectively, allowing the skin to cool faster. The weave also matters: looser weaves permit better air circulation, but if the fabric is too porous, it can allow heat to build up. The researchers emphasize that the optimal choice depends on a combination of these variables rather than simply weight or color.

These findings suggest that consumers and apparel designers should look beyond conventional descriptors like “light” or “loose.” By selecting fabrics engineered for moisture management and airflow, clothing can provide genuine relief in hot conditions. As the industry moves toward more performance‑oriented materials, consumers are encouraged to read technical specifications rather than rely solely on traditional summer‑wear clichés.
author: Medical Xpress
